subject: Physics

mods.t: Waves and the particle nature of light

cards: EDEXCEL-9PH0.IN_EQUILIBRIUM

State what is meant by ‘in equilibrium’.

[2 marks]

• sum of moments (about any point) is zero
• Or resultant moment is zero (about any point)
• sum of the forces (in any direction) is zero
• Or resultant force is zero (in any direction)
EDEXCEL-9PH0.VIRTUAL_IMAGE

State what is meant by a virtual image.

[1 mark]

• An image formed from the apparent divergence of light rays from a single point
• Or an image that cannot be projected on to a screen
EDEXCEL-9PH0.WAVEFRONT

State what is meant by a wavefront.

[1 mark]
Line/surface joining points on a wave that are in phase
EDEXCEL-9PH0.INELASTIC_COLLISION

A series of experiments was carried out in the 1970s to investigate the structure of protons using the linac at Stanford, USA. The collisions between electrons and the protons in these experiments are sometimes inelastic. State what is meant by an inelastic collision.

[1 mark]
(total) kinetic energy not conserved
EDEXCEL-9PH0.VECTOR_QUANTITY

Current density is a vector quantity. State what is meant by a vector quantity.

[1 mark]
A vector has magnitude and direction
EDEXCEL-9PH0.MOMENT_OF_A_FORCE_ABOUT_A_POINT

State what is meant by the moment of a force about a point.

[1 mark]

• Moment of a force (around a point) = force × perpendicular distance (to line of action of the force from the point)
• Or
• Moment of a force (around a point) = distance (to the point) × perpendicular component of force
Note: need to see “perpendicular” or equivalent
EDEXCEL-9PH0.ELASTIC_INTERACTION

Over one hundred years ago, Rutherford supervised a series of experiments using a source of alpha particles and thin gold foil. An elastic interaction occurs and the alpha particle recoils. State what is meant by an elastic interaction.

[1 mark]
(Total) kinetic energy conserved
EDEXCEL-9PH0.STANDARD_CANDLE

State what is meant by a standard candle.

[1 mark]
Object of known luminosity
EDEXCEL-9PH0.SUPERPOSITION_OF_WAVES

State what is meant by superposition of waves.

[2 marks]

• Two or more waves meet
• The (resultant) displacement (at a point) is the sum of the individual displacements from the individual waves
Not accepted: sum of amplitudes
EDEXCEL-9PH0.WITHIN_THE_ELASTIC_LIMIT

State what is meant by within the elastic limit.

[1 mark]

• (Within the elastic limit,) if the load is removed the specimen/spring will return to its original shape / length
• Or above the elastic limit the specimen remains permanently deformed if the load is removed
Also accept: the converse for each
EDEXCEL-9PH0.VIRTUAL_AND_UPRIGHT

The final image produced by the telescope is described as virtual and upright. State what is meant by virtual and upright.

[2 marks]

• Virtual means that the ray(s) of light do not pass through (the image position)
• Or Virtual means the image cannot be produced on a screen
• Upright means that the image is the same way up as the original object being observed
Also accept: same orientation (as original object)
Also accept: right way up
Not accepted: ‘not inverted’
EDEXCEL-9PH0.THRESHOLD_FREQUENCY

State what is meant by threshold frequency.

[1 mark]

The (minimum) frequency at/above which electrons are released
Also accept: frequency below which electrons are not released
EDEXCEL-9PH0.PHOTON

The photoelectric effect can be explained using the idea of photons. State what is meant by the term photon.

[1 mark]

• A **quantum** of (electromagnetic) energy/radiation
• Or
• A **discrete** packet of (electromagnetic) energy/radiation
Also accept: light for energy/radiation
EDEXCEL-9PH0.SPONTANEOUS_AND_RANDOM

State what is meant by spontaneous and random in the context of radioactive decay.

[2 marks]

• (Spontaneous) - independent of external conditions
• (Random) - cannot predict when a decay will occur
Also accept: cannot tell which nucleus will decay next
EDEXCEL-9PH0.ABSOLUTE_ZERO

State what is meant by absolute zero.

[1 mark]

The temperature at which the (mean) molecular kinetic energy is zero
Also accept: The lowest temperature possible
EDEXCEL-9PH0.POLARISED_LIGHT

An octopus can detect the orientation of polarised light. State what is meant by polarised light.

[2 marks]

• Either
• Polarised light is light where the oscillations are in a single plane
• Which includes the direction of propagation
• Or
• Polarised light is light where the oscillations are in a single direction
• Which is perpendicular to the direction of propagation
EDEXCEL-9PH0.PLANE_OF_POLARISATION_OF_LIGHT

Explain what is meant by the plane of polarisation of light.

[2 marks]

An explanation that makes reference to the following points:
• (The plane that) contains the oscillations / vibrations (of the wave)
• (The plane) including the direction of propagation of the wave
EDEXCEL-9PH0.ISOTOPES

State what is meant by isotopes.

[1 mark]

(isotopes are atoms/nuclides with the) same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons/nucleons (in the nucleus)
Not accepted: mass number or atomic number
Ignore: references to the number of electrons in the atoms
EDEXCEL-9PH0.PARTICLE_NATURE_OF_LIGHT

A student has been learning about the photoelectric effect. This experiment demonstrates the particle nature of light. Explain what is meant by the particle nature of light.

[2 marks]

• Light consists of (particles called) **photons**
These particles:
• are discrete packets of energy
• Or are quanta of energy
• Or have momentum
EDEXCEL-9PH0.SIMPLE_HARMONIC_MOTION

State what is meant by simple harmonic motion.

[2 marks]

The acceleration (of the platform) is:
• (directly) proportional to displacement from equilibrium position
• (always) acting towards the equilibrium position
• Or the idea that acceleration is in the opposite direction to displacement
• [An equation with symbols defined correctly is a valid response for both marks. e.g a ∝ -x or F ∝ -x]
Also accept: towards undisplaced point/fixed point/central point for equilibrium position
Also accept: a definition in terms of the force
i.e. the (resultant) force (on the platform) is:
(directly) proportional to displacement from equilibrium position
(always) acting towards the equilibrium position
Or the idea that force is in the opposite direction to displacement
EDEXCEL-9PH0.YIELD_POINT

State what is meant by yield point.

[1 mark]

• The value of stress at which the fishing line starts to deform permanently/plastically
• Or the value of stress at which the fishing line continues to extend with no additional force
Also accept: point / strain for “value of stress”
Also accept: line doesn’t return to original length when force is removed
EDEXCEL-9PH0.SPONTANEOUS_DECAY

State what is meant by spontaneous decay.

[1 mark]

• decay happens without any external stimulus
• Or decay is unaffected by external factors (such as temperature)
Not accepted: references to the randomness of the decay
EDEXCEL-9PH0.CENTRE_OF_GRAVITY_OF_AN_EXTENDED_BODY

State what is meant by the centre of gravity of an extended body.

[1 mark]

• the point through which the weight (of a body) acts
• Or The point around which the mass is equally distributed
• Or if supported at/below this point the body would be in equilibrium
Also accept: the point at which the entire mass can be assumed to be located.
EDEXCEL-9PH0.CRITICAL_ANGLE

State what is meant by critical angle.

[1 mark]

• the angle of incidence in an (optically) denser medium at which the angle of refraction (in the less dense medium) is 90°
• Or
• the greatest angle of incidence in an (optically) denser medium at which there is an emergent ray (into the less dense medium)
• Or
• the greatest angle of incidence in an (optically) denser medium at which there is a refracted ray (in the less dense medium)
Not accepted: answers stating or implying that the critical angle is the smallest angle at which total internal reflection occur, e.g., ‘The smallest angle at which t.i.r. takes place’, but do not automatically exclude answers on the basis of mentioning internal reflection alone without the inclusion of ‘total’
Not accepted: ‘The greatest angle before t.i.r. takes place’ is not sufficient
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_1_4_ACCURACY_PRECISION

A practical physics textbook states that “measurements may give a precise value for the quantity being determined but this may not necessarily be an accurate value”. Describe what physicists mean by the terms accuracy and precision.

[2 marks]

• Accuracy is (a measure of) how close a measured/calculated value is to the true value
• Precision is (a measure of) the consistency of values obtained by repeated measurements
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_1_5_ERROR_UNCERTAINTY_MEANING

A physics textbook states that “when carrying out experimental measurements there will always be errors and uncertainties”. Describe what physicists mean by error and by uncertainty.

[2 marks]

• An error is the difference between the (measured) result and the true value
• An uncertainty is the interval/range in which the (true) value can be considered to lie
Also accept: calculated/their for measured result/value
Also accept: theoretical/actual value for true value
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_1_5_REASONS_FOR_UNCERTAINTY

A physics textbook states that “when carrying out experimental measurements there will always be errors and uncertainties”. Give two reasons why a measurement may have an uncertainty.

[2 marks]

• Any **two** valid reasons that relate to
• the instrument being used to make the measurement
• the way in which the measurement is made
• the quantity measured not being constant
Not accepted: Vague statements that there will be random errors or there might be systematic errors
Note: Examples: resolution of instrument, zero error, parallax error, reaction time
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_9_6_KINETIC_THEORY_ASSUMPTION

State one assumption of the kinetic theory of gases.

[1 mark]

Any one from:
• Point particles
• Particles have negligible volume (compared to their container)
• Negligible forces between particles (except during a collision)
• Range of molecular forces small (in comparison to average separation)
• Duration of collisions negligible (in comparison to time between them)
• Newtonian mechanics applies
• Particles moves with uniform velocity between collisions
• Elastic collisions
• Particles move with (constant) random motion
Also accept: molecules for particles
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_8_1_RUTHERFORD_MODEL

Over one hundred years ago, Rutherford supervised a series of experiments using a source of alpha particles and thin gold foil. Describe the model of the atom that Rutherford proposed as a result of this series of experiments.

[3 marks]

• The atom is mainly empty space
• All/most of mass of the atom is in a nucleus/centre which is charged
• The nucleus is small compared to the atom
Also accept: dense and charged
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_8_1_MODEL_CHANGE_SCATTERING

At the beginning of the 20th century, Rutherford carried out large-angle alpha particle scattering experiments using gold foil. The vast majority of the alpha particles went straight through the foil whilst a few were deflected straight back. Describe how the model of the atom changed, as a consequence of these experiments.

[4 marks]

Before scattering experiment:
• atom containing equally distributed mass/charge
After experiment:
• very small nucleus containing (almost all) the mass of the atom
• atom mainly empty space
• nucleus is charged
Also accept: reference to ‘plum pudding model’
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_2_9_KILOWATT_HOUR_UNIT

Explain why the kilowatt-hour (kW h) is a unit of energy.

[2 marks]

• Quote P = E/t
• (k)W is unit of P and h unit of t so equivalent to E
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_3_4_NICHROME_RESISTANCE_TEMPERATURE

A student investigates how the resistance of a length of nichrome wire changes with temperature. Explain, in terms of particle behaviour, why the resistance of the nichrome wire changes as temperature increases.

[4 marks]

An explanation that makes reference to the following points:
• Kinetic energy of (lattice) ions increases
• or (Lattice) ions vibrate with greater amplitude
• The frequency of collisions between electrons and ions increases
• (Drift) velocity of electrons decreases, so current decreases (for the same p.d.)
• So resistance of nichrome wire increases
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_3_3_THERMISTOR_RESISTANCE_TEMPERATURE

A student wants to investigate how the resistance R of a negative temperature coefficient thermistor varies with its temperature T. Explain, in terms of particle behaviour, why the resistance of the thermistor decreases as temperature increases.

[4 marks]

• Increased temperature causes more energy transfer to lattice ions / atoms
• More charge carriers released / available
• I = nAvq, so relative increase in I
• Reference to R = V / I to justify decrease in R
Also accept: reverse argument
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_8_2_HIGH_ENERGY_ELECTRONS_PROTON

Explain why electrons need high energies to investigate the structure of a proton.

[2 marks]

• High energy electrons will have a short (de Broglie) wavelength
• The wavelength needs to be comparable/smaller than proton size
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_8_3_HIGH_ENERGY_COLLISIONS_HIGGS

The Higgs particle was discovered using the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) in 2012. Two beams of very high energy protons, moving in opposite directions, were made to collide. Explain the need for such high energy collisions.

[3 marks]

• Energy (of protons) converted to mass (of Higgs)
• or Energy is required to overcome electrostatic repulsion between protons
• Reference to E = mc^{2} (can be written in any form)
• Because c^{2} is very large (E must be large)
• or Higgs particle is massive so needs a lot of energy to create it
Also accept: Alternative based on numerical values: Observation that Higgs mass is 120 GeV/c^{2}
Also accept: This requires an energy of at least 120 GeV
Also accept: Each beam of protons would need an energy of at least 60 GeV
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_11_2_RADON_HAZARD

Radon is a radioactive gas. One isotope of radon decays to polonium, Po, by emitting an alpha particle. Radon is produced in the ground and escapes into the atmosphere. Explain why this is a safety hazard.

[2 marks]

• Radon gas can be breathed in and can cause damage to living cells
• or Once radon is inside the body the alpha particles/radiation can cause damage to living cells
• Because alpha (particles) highly ionising
Also accept: the idea of damage e.g. causing mutations/cancer etc. Must have stated that this happens inside the body
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_10_4_MAIN_SEQUENCE_STABILITY

Explain why main sequence stars do not collapse due to gravitational forces.

[2 marks]

An explanation that makes reference to the following points:
• Fusion takes place (from hydrogen to helium)
• This releases energy and leads to an (outward) pressure/force which balances gravitational forces
Also accept: high temperature for energy
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_8_4_LAMBDA_NOT_DIRECTLY_OBSERVED

The neutral lambda λ0 particle is a baryon of mass 1116 MeV/c^{2} and contains one strange quark. The λ0 particle cannot be directly observed in particle experiments, however some of the decay products can. Explain why the λ0 particle cannot be directly observed but information about it can be obtained by studying its decay particles.

[3 marks]

• Neutral particles do not leave a track/ionise
• Reference to conservation laws to deduce the properties of particles
• Tracks of decay particles can determine momentum of lambda particle
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_5_9_VARYING_STRING_TENSION

A student carries out an experiment using a guitar string. She investigates the effect of varying the tension in the guitar string on the frequency of sound produced when the string is plucked. Describe a method of varying and measuring the tension in the string.

[2 marks]

• Use a pulley and set of masses/weights hung on string
• Tension = weight (of set of masses) or T=mg
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_5_4_REFRACTION_ACCURACY_PRECAUTIONS

A student is carrying out an experiment to identify which type of glass a rectangular block is made from. The student shines a ray of light onto one surface of the rectangular block. The student marks the path of the ray on paper. He takes corresponding measurements of the angle of incidence i and the angle of refraction r at the air-glass interface. State two precautions the student should take to improve the accuracy of these measurements.

[2 marks]

• Max 2
• Use large angles of incidence or use a wide range of angles
• Use narrowest possible ray
• Repeat and calculate mean
• Work in a dark room.
• Use monochromatic light
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_11_6_FUSION_CONDITIONS_STARS

Nuclear fusion involves small nuclei joining to make larger nuclei. Nuclear fission involves large nuclei splitting to become smaller nuclei. Both of these processes release energy. Explain the conditions required to bring about and maintain nuclear fusion.

[3 marks]

An explanation that makes reference to:
• Identifies (very) high temperature **and** (very) high density
• (Very) high temperature to provide enough energy to overcome the (electrostatic) repulsive force between nuclei
• (Very) high density to give big enough collision rate to maintain reaction
Also accept: pressure for density in MP1
Also accept: correct reference to strong force
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_5_6_ULTRASOUND_PULSES

Scientists can use a pulse‑echo technique with ultrasound to detect plastic in the oceans. A transducer that emits and detects ultrasound pulses is positioned just below the surface of the water. Give a reason why the ultrasound is emitted in short pulses.

[1 mark]
So reflected pulse returns before next pulse is transmitted
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_5_6_ULTRASOUND_HIGH_FREQUENCY

Scientists can use a pulse‑echo technique with ultrasound to detect plastic in the oceans. A transducer that emits and detects ultrasound pulses is positioned just below the surface of the water. Explain why small pieces of plastic are more likely to be detected by using ultrasound with a high frequency.

[2 marks]

• High frequency has a short wavelength
• Short wavelengths diffract less around smaller objects
• Or greater amount of detail can be detected
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_2_4_BENDING_KNEES_LANDING

Some sports place high stresses on the bones in the body, which can result in injury. Explain how bending both knees when landing helps the gymnast prevent an injury.

[3 marks]

• bending knees increases the time to come to rest
• decreasing rate of change of momentum or reducing the deceleration
• and (hence) force
Also accept: converse argument
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_5_2_LASER_SAFETY

In an experiment to demonstrate interference of light, monochromatic light from a laser is shone onto two narrow slits. A series of light and dark lines is observed on a screen placed a distance away from the slits. State one safety precaution that should be taken with this procedure.

[1 mark]
Do not stare into laser
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_8_2_COSMIC_RAY_LAMBDA

Lambda particles were first detected in experiments which made use of cosmic rays entering the atmosphere. Cosmic rays are mainly high‑energy protons which have a mass less than that of a lambda particle. Explain why a cosmic ray could lead to the creation of a lambda particle.

[2 marks]

• Energy of cosmic ray could be turned into matter/mass
• According to ΔE = c^{2}Δm
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_8_2_STANDARD_MODEL_PION_MUON

A negatively charged pion decays into a muon and an antineutrino. According to the standard model, the pion and muon are classified within two different groups of particles. State which group each particle belongs to and describe the two groups.

[4 marks]

• Muon is a lepton
• Muons / leptons are fundamental particles
• Pion is a meson
• Pions / mesons consist of a quark and antiquark
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_7_1_BEE_HAIR_ELECTRIC_FIELD

Flowers can attract bees by being colourful or by producing a scent. Some flowers also attract bees by producing an electric field. It is suggested that the hairs on a bee deflect slightly when close to the flower. Explain what would cause a hair to deflect in an electric field.

[2 marks]

• Hair must be charged
• As an electric field exerts a force on a charge
Also accept: “negative” or “positive”
Also accept: as like charges repel Or opposite charges attract
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_8_2_DELTA_IS_BARYON

A delta particle decays into a proton and a pion. State why the delta particle must be classified as a baryon based on the evidence of its decay.

[1 mark]

• baryon number conserved
• Or baryon number is +1 on both sides of equation
• Or proton is baryon and the pion is not a baryon
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_8_2_SIGMA_DECAY_CONSERVATION

A sigma ( ∑+ ) particle is a baryon. It can decay into a positive pion and a neutron. Explain whether the conservation laws of charge and baryon number are obeyed for this decay.

[2 marks]

• Charge: +1 → +1 + 0
• Baryon number: 1 → 0 + 1
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_4_1_STOKES_LAW_CONDITIONS

State two conditions that determine whether Stokes' law applies to a moving object.

[2 marks]

• Any two from
• Small object
• spherical object
• (Moving at a) slow speed
• In laminar flow or not turbulent flow
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_5_1_SOUND_PRESSURE_VARIATIONS

Describe how the displacement of air molecules causes pressure variations in the air.

[3 marks]

• Longitudinal wave
• Or Oscillations of air molecules are parallel to the direction of the energy transfer
• Creating compressions **and** rarefactions
• Or Creating regions where the molecules are close together **and** regions where they are further apart
• Molecules close together create higher pressure
• Or molecules further apart create lower pressure
• Or compressions are areas of high pressure
• Or rarefactions are areas of low pressure
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_5_5_DEMONSTRATE_PLANE_OF_POLARISATION

The light emitted from a laptop screen is plane polarised. Explain how the plane of polarisation of the emitted light can be demonstrated using a polarising filter.

[3 marks]

• Rotate filter or laptop and brightness of the screen varies
• Either
• When screen goes dark plane of polarised light is perpendicular to the plane of polarisation of the filter
• As polarised light from the screen is absorbed by the filter.
• Or
• When screen is brightest plane of polarised light is parallel to the plane of polarisation of the filter
• As polarised light from the screen is transmitted by the filter.
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_5_1_LIGHT_TRANSVERSE_WAVE

Describe how light is transmitted as a transverse wave.

[2 marks]

• Light is an electromagnetic wave
• Or light is oscillations of electric and magnetic fields
• Oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_5_5_HUYGENS_DIFFRACTION_GAP

Diffraction provides evidence for the wave nature of light. Use Huygens' construction to describe what happens to light waves after passing through a narrow gap.

[3 marks]

• The wave spreads out (after passing through a gap)
• Each point on the wave acts as a source of secondary wavelets
• That interfere/superpose
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_10_1_PARALLAX_LIMIT

Explain why trigonometric parallax is not used beyond a certain distance.

[2 marks]

• The (parallax) angle becomes very small
• Or the diameter of the Earth's orbit is very small
• Giving a (very) large percentage uncertainty
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_10_2_DISTANCE_BEYOND_STANDARD_CANDLES

Describe how distances too large for the use of standard candles can be determined.

[3 marks]

• Measure change in wavelength / frequency
• Determine relative velocity using redshift formula
• Then apply v = H0d
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_11_2_DECAY_CONSTANT_DESPITE_RANDOM

Explain why the decay constant of an isotope can be determined even though nuclear decay is random.

[2 marks]

• The probability of decay (in a specified time) may be determined
• (Probability may be applied accurately because) very large numbers are involved
Also accept: For MP1 accept reference to the proportion of nuclei decaying at a specified time
EDEXCEL-9PH0.R_5_7_THRESHOLD_NOT_WAVE_THEORY

Explain why the observation of a threshold frequency is not consistent with the wave theory of light.

[2 marks]

• With waves, energy would build up
• A photoelectron would (eventually have enough energy to) be emitted with any frequency, (which is not observed)
